intro: Scarbo, marked Modéré, is the third piece of Ravel’s Gaspard de la nuit. Scarbo is the creature who scratches at the bed curtains, vanishes and comes back larger than the room, and Ravel writes soft repeated notes, very wide leaps and long silences for him.

sections.label: A · Low opening figure, repeated notes
sections.mNote: A repeated-note figure follows the low opening figure.

sections.label: B · Vif, leaps across the keyboard
sections.mNote: Vif. The two hands move apart in leaps.

sections.label: Dev · Repeated notes and rising chords
sections.mNote: Short figures return in wider leaps and chords.

sections.label: A′ · Opening figure returns in the bass
sections.mNote: The opening drumming figure moves down into the bass.

sections.label: B′ · Return of the dance
sections.mNote: Quick figures emerge from the low repeated notes.

sections.label: Dev · Final chords of the development
sections.mNote: Leaps and repeated chords fill the keyboard.

sections.label: Coda · Quiet repeated chords
sections.mNote: Quiet repeated chords stop without slowing.

cues.title: Opening of Scarbo
cues.text: Three low notes rise in the piano. A soft repeated note sounds beneath a held chord, then stops. Ravel puts a fermata over the silence and marks it très long (very long).
cues.evidence: Durand score (1909), plate D. & F. 7207, p. 23: opening low figure, très fondu, en trémolo, and très long fermata. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/6/6a/IMSLP246875-PMLP02576-Ravel,_Maurice-Gaspard_de_la_nuit_Durand_7207_scan.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Acceleration to Vif
cues.text: The piano accelerates through rising figures to Vif. The hands move far apart and play bass notes and high chords at the same quick tempo. Sudden rests interrupt the passage.
cues.evidence: Durand score, pp. 23–24: En accélérant, Vif, widely separated hands and rests after the first outburst.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Scarbo in Bertrand’s poem
cues.text: Bertrand’s narrator hears Scarbo laughing in his alcove, then “grincer son ongle sur la soie des courtines de mon lit” — “his nail scraping the silk curtains of my bed”. The dwarf spins on one foot and rolls around the room like a witch’s dropped spindle.
cues.evidence: Aloysius Bertrand, Scarbo, Gaspard de la nuit, Mercure de France edition (1895), pp. 247–248, second and third paragraphs; our translation. https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Gaspard_de_la_nuit_(%C3%A9d._1895)/Scarbo_2

cues.title: Rising three-note figure
cues.text: The rising three-note figure of the opening returns in new octaves. Repeated notes and leaps carry much of the writing, and the small figures expand into large groups of chords.
cues.evidence: Durand score, pp. 23–42: recurring rising three-note figure, repeated-note writing and octave displacement.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Return of the opening
cues.text: The opening returns with its low three-note figure, held chord and repeated notes. This time the repeated notes lie lower in the bass. Ravel marks the soft pedal and writes almost nothing in the upper register of the piano.
cues.evidence: Durand score, pp. 34–35: reprise of the opening, sourdine, low repeated notes and subsequent ppp bass writing.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Bertrand’s “Scarbo”, fourth paragraph
cues.text: In Bertrand’s poem the dwarf grows between the narrator and the moon “comme le clocher d’une cathédrale gothique” — “like the tower of a Gothic cathedral”. A little golden bell shakes on his pointed cap.
cues.evidence: Bertrand, Scarbo, Mercure de France edition (1895), p. 248, fourth paragraph; our translation. https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Gaspard_de_la_nuit_(%C3%A9d._1895)/Scarbo_2

cues.title: Final bars, Sans ralentir
cues.text: The piano plays ppp repeated chords, then a final run up the keyboard. Ravel marks the passage Sans ralentir, without slowing. Bertrand’s poem ends “et soudain il s’éteignait”, “and suddenly he went out”, like a candle.
cues.evidence: Durand score, p. 42: ppp repeated chords and Sans ralentir. Bertrand, Scarbo, final sentence, Mercure de France edition (1895), p. 248; our translation. https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Gaspard_de_la_nuit_(%C3%A9d._1895)/Scarbo_2
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: From held silences to Vif
transitions.from: A · Low opening figure, repeated notes
transitions.to: B · Vif, leaps across the keyboard
transitions.how: After the held silences, rising figures in the piano accelerate. At Vif the hands move apart, with low notes alternating with high chords, and a crescendo runs from pp to ff. Two bars of rests break off the passage, and then the moving accompaniment resumes.
transitions.evidence: Durand score (1909), pp. 23–24: En accélérant, Vif, crescendo and rests.

transitions.title: The low three notes return
transitions.from: Dev · Repeated notes and rising chords
transitions.to: A′ · Opening figure returns in the bass
transitions.how: The running figures stop, and the three low notes of the opening return under the soft pedal. The held chord and the repeated-note figure follow them, with another fermata. Ravel then moves the repeated notes down into the bass at ppp.
transitions.evidence: Durand score, pp. 34–35: return of the introduction and its descent into the bass.

transitions.title: The chords become a flicker
transitions.from: Dev · Final chords of the development
transitions.how: The wide arpeggios contract into quiet repeated chords above a low held bass. The pianist moves through short rests and little answering figures, then darts upwards to the last note. Sans ralentir keeps the ending quick.
transitions.evidence: Durand score, p. 42: ppp repeated chords, low pedal, final short figures and Sans ralentir.

composer.epithet: Composer of a ballet built from two tunes and a snare drum, and of a suite of dances dedicated to his war dead.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1889; Fauré for composition, André Gedalge for counterpoint
Ricardo Viñes · Maurice Delage · Tristan Klingsor · M. D. Calvocoressi
Le Belvédère, Montfort-l’Amaury, 1921–37; now a museum
Two operas, two piano concertos, ballets, songs, chamber and piano music; no symphony

quote.text: Does it never occur to these people that I may be artificial by nature?
quote.source: To M. D. Calvocoressi, recalled in his Musicians Gallery (1933)

composer.background:
Ravel’s father took his sons to factories to see the machinery, and his mother sang to them. Pierre-Joseph was a Swiss-born engineer; Marie Delouart was Basque and had grown up in Madrid. Maurice was born in Ciboure on 7 March 1875, and the family moved to Paris three months later. He went back to the Basque coast many times. Spain appears often in his music, in the plucked-guitar attacks of Alborada del gracioso, the habanera in the Rapsodie espagnole and the clocks of a Toledo clockmaker’s shop in L’heure espagnole.

He entered the Paris Conservatoire at fourteen, studied piano with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot and lost his place in 1895 for failing to win the required prizes. André Gedalge gave him counterpoint lessons from 1897, and in January 1898 he entered the composition class of Fauré. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, gave the first performances of Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit, pieces he could not have played himself with comparable command.
